common_name: Candy Mountain Foxglove (Extra-Large All-Around Flowering Foxglove)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter or sow in a nursery bed in summer for bloom the following year; Candy Mountain bears exceptionally large flowers arranged all the way around the spike rather than facing one direction, as most foxglove cultivars do.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; as a biennial, it forms a low rosette of foliage the first year and sends up flower spikes the following spring before dying, though it self-seeds readily to maintain a colony. Candy Mountain bears unusually large, densely packed flowers in soft rose-pink arranged evenly all the way around the flower spike rather than facing to one side, giving a fuller, more symmetrical presence than most foxglove cultivars when viewed from any angle. Bees, especially bumblebees, visit the tubular flowers heavily. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where pets or children might handle it, and stake tall flower spikes in exposed, windy locations.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in early spring, or plant divisions, into lean, very well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; sunset foxglove is a true perennial species, unlike the biennial common foxglove.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since this Mediterranean species is far more likely to be lost to wet winter soil than to drought. Sunset foxglove, native to dry hillsides of Spain and North Africa, bears unusual, small, tubular flowers in warm coppery-orange to russet-brown shades with darker reticulated veining inside the throat, a departure from the pinks, purples, and whites typical of common foxglove. As a true short-lived perennial rather than a biennial, it can persist and rebloom for a few years in the lean, dry, well-drained conditions of a rock garden or gravel bed. All parts are toxic if ingested. Cut back spent flower spikes to tidy the plant, and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which shortens its lifespan considerably.

common_name: Pink Truffles Baptisia (Decadence Series Dusty Pink False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Pink Truffles is a compact Decadence-series hybrid with unusual dusty mauve-pink flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Pink Truffles bears dense spikes of unusual, dusty mauve-pink, pea-like flowers, a soft, muted color rarely seen in the genus, on a compact, upright plant that is part of the Decadence series bred for more manageable garden size than the sprawling wild Baptisia species while keeping the genus's legendary toughness and longevity. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the plant serves as a larval host for several native butterfly species. It is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established. Avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants; simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.
